title: Strategy or State, and a sealed switch

questions.stem: The page's TrafficLight is a State, while its Sorter is a Strategy. What makes TrafficLight a State and not a Strategy?

options.text: Its behaviour lives in a field that another object can replace at runtime.
options.says: Sorter keeps its strategy in a replaceable field too; the two patterns share that structure, so it cannot tell them apart.

options.text: Its held object has a single method, where a strategy may offer several.
options.says: The page puts it the other way round: a strategy often has one method, and a state usually has several, one per action.

options.text: Its current object chooses the next one, instead of the client choosing.
options.says: In State the state object decides the transition as part of normal operation; in Strategy the client chooses and changes the algorithm.

questions.stem: `PaymentStrategy` is sealed, and `describe()` switches over it with one case per permitted record and no `default`. A fourth record, `BankTransfer`, is added to the `permits` clause. What happens?

options.text: It compiles, and describe() throws MatchException for a BankTransfer.
options.says: The compiler checks the switch against the permitted subtypes, so the gap is reported before the program can run.

options.text: It fails to compile until describe() gets a BankTransfer case.
options.says: An exhaustive switch over a sealed interface must cover every permitted type, so a new strategy without a case is a compile error.

options.text: It compiles, and describe() returns null for a BankTransfer.
options.says: A switch expression never quietly yields null for an unmatched value; here the missing case is a compile-time error.
